en: Please come in and have a seat.
context: Welcoming a guest at home.
explain: This is a warm invitation. 'Have a seat' is a polite way to say sit down.
usage: Use it when a guest or visitor arrives.
leelaQ: A relative visits your house. How do you welcome them?
answer: Please come in and have a seat.

en: I would rather stay at home today, if you don't mind.
tamil: உங்களுக்கு பிரச்சனை இல்லன்னா இன்னிக்கு நான் வீட்டுலயே இருக்கறேன்.
context: Politely declining an outing.
explain: 'I would rather' shows your preference. 'If you don't mind' keeps it soft.
usage: Use it with friends or family when you do not want to go out.
leelaQ: Friends plan a movie but you are tired. What do you say?
answer: I would rather stay at home today, if you don't mind.

en: Can you lend me some money till Friday?
tamil: வெள்ளிக்கிழமை வரைக்கும் கொஞ்சம் காசு கடன் தர முடியுமா?
context: Asking a close friend for money.
explain: 'Lend' is what the giver does, 'borrow' is what you do. 'Till Friday' gives a clear time.
usage: Use it only with close friends or family.
leelaQ: You need small money until salary day. What do you ask a friend?
answer: Can you lend me some money till Friday? I will return it.

en: May I ask you a small favour?
tamil: நான் உங்ககிட்ட ஒரு சின்ன உதவி கேக்கலாமா?
context: Starting a request with a neighbour.
explain: This sentence opens the conversation before the real request. It prepares the listener.
usage: Use it before asking something bigger from a neighbour or colleague.
leelaQ: Before asking your neighbour for help, what do you say first?
answer: May I ask you a small favour?

en: Could you give me a lift to the station?
context: Asking a colleague with a bike or car.
explain: 'Give me a lift' means take me in your vehicle.
usage: Use it with colleagues or neighbours who are going the same way.
leelaQ: It is raining and you have no auto. What do you ask your colleague?
answer: Could you give me a lift to the station? It is raining.

en: I will be glad to join you for lunch.
context: Accepting a lunch invitation.
explain: 'I will be glad to' is a polite and warm way to accept.
usage: Use it to accept invitations from colleagues or friends.
leelaQ: A colleague invites you for lunch. How do you accept?
answer: I will be glad to join you for lunch.

en: Please don't be angry, it was my mistake.
tamil: தயவு செய்து கோபப்படாதீங்க, அது என் தப்பு.
context: Apologising to a friend.
explain: This sentence says sorry and accepts blame. 'Don't be angry' is a soft request.
usage: Use it when you did something wrong and want to calm the person.
leelaQ: You forgot a friend's birthday. What do you say?
answer: Please don't be angry, it was my mistake.

en: Is it okay if I bring my friend along?
context: Asking a host about bringing a friend.
explain: 'Is it okay if ...?' is a casual way to ask for permission.
usage: Use it with a host before taking another person to an event.
leelaQ: You are invited to a dinner. How do you ask about a friend?
answer: Is it okay if I bring my friend along?

en: Kindly send your reply as soon as possible.
context: Writing a formal email request.
explain: 'Kindly' is formal and common in Indian office English.
usage: Use it in formal emails to ask for a quick response.
leelaQ: How do you end an email asking for a fast answer?
answer: Kindly send your reply as soon as possible.

en: Shall I say that once more, slowly?
tamil: நான் அதை இன்னொரு தடவ மெதுவா சொல்லட்டுமா?
context: Offering to repeat for a student.
explain: 'Shall I ...?' offers help without forcing it.
usage: Use it as a teacher or senior when someone looks confused.
leelaQ: Your friend did not follow your instructions. What do you offer?
answer: Shall I say that once more, slowly? I spoke too fast.

en: Can I take a message for him?
context: Answering a phone call for a colleague.
explain: 'Take a message' means write down what the caller wants to say.
usage: Use it when the person the caller wants is not available.
leelaQ: Someone calls for your absent boss. What do you offer?
answer: Can I take a message for him? I will tell him.

en: I'm sorry, but he is not available right now.
context: Telling a caller politely.
explain: 'Not available' is a polite phrase for not here or busy.
usage: Use it at reception or on the phone for a colleague who is out.
leelaQ: A caller asks for someone who is out. What do you say?
answer: I'm sorry, but he is not available right now.

en: Could you turn the music down a little?
context: Asking a neighbour about loud music.
explain: 'Turn down' means reduce the volume. 'A little' keeps it kind.
usage: Use it with neighbours or family members when noise is a problem.
leelaQ: The neighbour plays loud music late at night. What do you ask?
answer: Could you turn the music down a little? I am studying.

en: Please take your seat, the class will start soon.
tamil: தயவு செய்து உங்க இடத்துல உக்காருங்க, வகுப்பு சீக்கிரம் தொடங்கும்.
context: A teacher asking students to sit.
explain: 'Take your seat' is a polite way to say sit down.
usage: Use it as a teacher or trainer before starting a session.
leelaQ: You are the teacher and students are standing. What do you say?
answer: Please take your seat, the class will start soon.

en: Do you want me to book the tickets?
context: Offering to book tickets for family.
explain: 'Do you want me to ...?' is a simple offer in everyday talk.
usage: Use it with family or friends when you can do a task for them.
leelaQ: Your family plans a trip. What do you offer to do?
answer: Do you want me to book the tickets? I will do it now.

en: I would really appreciate your help with this.
tamil: இதுல உங்க உதவியை நான் ரொம்ப மதிப்பேன்.
context: Asking a senior for help.
explain: 'I would appreciate' is a formal and respectful way to ask for help.
usage: Use it with seniors or clients when you need real support.
leelaQ: You need your senior's help on a hard task. What do you say?
answer: I would really appreciate your help with this.

en: Sorry, you can't park your vehicle here.
context: A security guard refusing politely.
explain: 'Sorry' makes a rule sound softer. 'Can't' tells what is not allowed.
usage: Use it as a guard or staff member to stop someone politely.
leelaQ: A visitor parks in a no-parking area. What do you say as the guard?
answer: Sorry, you can't park your vehicle here, sir.

en: Could I speak to the manager, please?
context: Asking at a shop or hotel.
explain: 'Could I speak to ...?' is the polite way to ask for a person on the phone or in person.
usage: Use it when you have a complaint or need a decision.
leelaQ: Your order is wrong. Whom do you ask to speak to?
answer: Could I speak to the manager, please?

en: Please share the notes with me when you are free.
tamil: நீங்க ஃப்ரீயா இருக்கும்போது அந்த நோட்ஸை எனக்கு ஷேர் பண்ணுங்க.
context: Asking a classmate for notes.
explain: 'When you are free' gives the other person freedom, so it sounds kind.
usage: Use it with classmates or colleagues for non-urgent requests.
leelaQ: You missed a class. How do you ask a friend for notes?
answer: Please share the notes with me when you are free.

en: I can drop you at your place if you want.
tamil: நீங்க விரும்பினா உங்க வீட்டுல உங்களை விடறேன்.
context: Offering a ride home to a friend.
explain: 'If you want' makes the offer optional and friendly.
usage: Use it with friends or colleagues after a late meeting.
leelaQ: It is late and your friend has no ride. What do you offer?
answer: I can drop you at your place if you want.

en: Would you be able to attend the meeting tomorrow?
context: Asking a colleague to attend.
explain: 'Would you be able to ...?' is polite for asking about someone's availability.
usage: Use it at work to check availability before fixing a plan.
leelaQ: You want a teammate at tomorrow's meeting. What do you ask?
answer: Would you be able to attend the meeting tomorrow?

en: No, thank you, I have already eaten.
context: Refusing second serving politely.
explain: 'No, thank you' is a clear and polite refusal. 'Already' shows it is done.
usage: Use it at a feast or party when the host keeps offering food.
leelaQ: A host offers more rice but you are full. What do you say?
answer: No, thank you, I have already eaten enough.

en: Could you check my answer sheet once again?
tamil: என் விடைத்தாளை இன்னொரு தடவை பாக்க முடியுமா?
context: Asking a teacher to recheck marks.
explain: 'Once again' is polite when asking for a second look.
usage: Use it with a teacher or examiner when you feel a mistake was made.
leelaQ: You think your marks are wrong. What do you ask the teacher?
answer: Could you check my answer sheet once again, madam?

en: Do tell me if there is anything you need.
context: Offering help to a new neighbour.
explain: 'Do tell me' makes the offer warm and sincere.
usage: Use it with guests, new neighbours or hotel customers.
leelaQ: Your new neighbour is moving in. What do you tell them?
answer: Do tell me if there is anything you need. I live next door.

en: Is it all right if I call you after dinner?
context: Asking permission to call later.
explain: 'Is it all right if ...?' is a gentle way to ask permission.
usage: Use it with elders or colleagues when you want to call at a better time.
leelaQ: You want to call your uncle later. How do you ask?
answer: Is it all right if I call you after dinner?
